subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Ultimatum Game
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Ultimatum Game.

hook.text: You get $100 to split with a stranger. You offer $1. The stranger rejects it. You both get nothing.

buildup.text: In the ultimatum game, responders reject unfair offers even when rejection costs them money. Fairness overrides profit.

discovery.text: Across all cultures, offers below 20% are usually rejected. People pay a real cost to punish perceived unfairness.

twist.text: Proposers anticipate this. Most offer 40-50% because they know unfair splits will be rejected.

climax.text: Standard economics assumed humans maximize money. The ultimatum game proved humans maximize fairness, even at a cost.

punchline.text: People will burn money to punish unfairness.

quiz.question: Why do responders reject low offers in the ultimatum game?
options: They misunderstand the rules of the game
They prefer nothing over accepting an unfair split

details.summary: In the ultimatum game, one player proposes a split of money and the other accepts or rejects. Rejection means both get nothing. Economically rational players should accept any offer, but people routinely reject offers below 20 percent as unfairly low.
details.whyItMatters: The ultimatum game demolished the assumption of pure self-interest in economics. It proved that fairness is a fundamental human motivation, powerful enough that people will destroy value to punish perceived injustice.
takeaways: Most proposers offer 40 to 50 percent, not the rational minimum
Offers below 20 percent are rejected about half the time
Rejection sacrifices money to punish unfairness, defying pure self-interest

faq.question: Why do people reject low offers in the ultimatum game?
faq.answer: Low offers trigger a strong emotional response of indignation and perceived disrespect. Brain imaging shows rejection activates regions associated with disgust. People prefer zero to accepting what feels like exploitation, even though rejection is economically irrational.

faq.question: Why do proposers offer more than the minimum?
faq.answer: Partially from genuine fairness preferences and partially from strategic fear of rejection. Proposers know low offers will likely be rejected, so offering 40 to 50 percent maximizes expected payoff while satisfying fairness norms.
